questions.q: A company needs separate billing for each department. What should it create for each department?
questions.why: A subscription is a billing boundary and an access boundary. Departments often get their own subscription, grouped under management groups.

questions.q: Match each Azure scope to its description.
rows: Groups subscriptions so policy and access apply to all of them
Billing and access boundary
Logical container for resources that share a lifecycle
A single VM, storage account or database
questions.why: Management groups hold subscriptions, subscriptions hold resource groups, resource groups hold resources.

questions.q: Which TWO resources are created along with an Azure virtual machine?
opts: A disk for the operating system
questions.why: A VM needs compute size, storage disks and networking: a virtual network, a network interface and optionally a public IP address.

questions.q: You need to run a single container quickly with no orchestration or VMs to manage. Which service fits?
questions.why: Container Instances is the simplest way to run a container. AKS orchestrates many containers.

questions.q: Which provides Windows desktops and apps hosted in Azure that users reach from any device?
questions.why: Azure Virtual Desktop is desktop and app virtualization in the cloud, with multi-session Windows.

questions.q: A web app should be reachable only from your virtual network, using a private IP address. What should you use?
questions.why: A private endpoint gives a service a private IP address in your virtual network (through Private Link), so traffic stays off the public internet.

questions.q: Two virtual networks in different regions must talk to each other over the Microsoft backbone. What should you configure?
questions.why: Peering connects virtual networks, including across regions (global peering), over Microsoft's backbone.

questions.q: You need a private, dedicated connection from your datacenter to Azure that does not cross the public internet. What should you use?
questions.why: ExpressRoute is a private connection through a connectivity provider. A VPN gateway sends encrypted traffic over the public internet.

questions.q: Data must be kept for at least 180 days and is almost never read. Retrieval can take hours. Which access tier costs least?
questions.why: Archive has the lowest storage cost but is offline: data must be rehydrated, which takes hours. Minimum retention 180 days.

questions.q: Match each access tier to its minimum recommended retention.
rows: Cool
Cold
Archive
questions.why: Cool 30, cold 90, archive 180. Hot has no minimum. Moving data out early incurs an early deletion charge.

questions.q: Which redundancy option keeps three copies in three availability zones of the primary region only?
questions.why: ZRS spreads three copies across zones in one region. LRS keeps three copies in one datacenter. GRS and GZRS add a secondary region.

questions.q: You need geo-redundancy AND the ability to read data from the secondary region at any time. Which option?
questions.why: The RA (read-access) versions, RA-GRS and RA-GZRS, let you read from the secondary region without a failover.

questions.q: Which storage account type is recommended for most scenarios and supports blobs, files, queues and tables?
questions.why: Standard general-purpose v2 covers most scenarios. Premium accounts are for low-latency workloads of one type.

questions.q: You must copy files to Azure Blob Storage from a command line script. Which tool fits?
questions.why: AzCopy is a command-line tool. Storage Explorer is a graphical app. File Sync keeps on-premises file servers in sync with Azure Files.

questions.q: Branch offices want their Windows file servers to cache Azure file shares locally. Which service?
questions.why: Azure File Sync turns a Windows Server into a local cache of an Azure file share.

questions.q: You must move 60 TB of data to Azure but the internet link is slow. What should you use?
questions.why: Data Box is a physical device (up to 80 TB) shipped to you, filled, and returned to Microsoft for upload.

questions.q: A legacy app needs domain join, Group Policy and Kerberos, but you do not want to run domain controllers in Azure. What should you use?
questions.why: Entra Domain Services provides managed domain services (domain join, Group Policy, LDAP, Kerberos and NTLM) without you deploying domain controllers.

questions.q: Partner company staff must sign in to your app using their own work accounts. Which feature?
questions.why: External identities let people outside your organization use their own identities to reach your apps.

questions.q: Users sign in once and then reach Microsoft 365, the Azure portal and other apps without signing in again. What is this?
questions.why: SSO means one sign-in, one set of credentials, many apps.

questions.q: Which TWO are passwordless authentication methods in Azure?
opts: A password plus an SMS code
questions.why: Passwordless methods include Windows Hello for Business, the Microsoft Authenticator app and FIDO2 security keys (passkeys).

questions.q: A user needs to restart VMs in one resource group but nothing else. Which feature grants exactly that?
opts: Azure role-based access control (RBAC) at the resource group scope
questions.why: RBAC assigns a role at a scope. Least privilege means the narrowest role at the narrowest scope.

questions.q: Developers must be prevented from creating resources outside the East US region. What should you use?
questions.why: Azure Policy enforces rules about how resources are configured, such as allowed regions, and can deny non-compliant deployments.

questions.q: A production database must not be deleted by accident, even by an Owner. What should you apply?
questions.why: Locks apply to everyone, including Owners. A Delete lock allows changes but blocks deletion. ReadOnly blocks both.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: A resource lock applies even to users with the Owner role.
To delete a resource with a Delete lock, you must first remove the lock.
A ReadOnly lock still allows the resource to be deleted.
questions.why: Locks override RBAC permissions for everyone. Remove the lock first. ReadOnly blocks changes AND deletion.

questions.q: Match each requirement to the right tool.
rows: Only allow VM sizes from an approved list
Stop anyone deleting a storage account
Give the help desk permission to restart VMs
Group costs by department on the bill
questions.why: Policy controls HOW resources are configured. Locks stop change or deletion. RBAC controls WHO can do what. Tags add metadata for cost and organization.

questions.q: What is an Azure Policy initiative?
opts: A lock applied to a whole subscription
A tag that is inherited by every resource
A group of related policy definitions assigned together
questions.why: Initiatives bundle policies toward one goal, such as a compliance standard, so you assign and track them as one.

questions.q: Which service gives a unified view to discover, classify and govern data across on-premises, multicloud and SaaS?
questions.why: Microsoft Purview is a family of data governance, risk and compliance solutions with one view of your data estate.

questions.q: Which TWO factors affect the cost of Azure resources?
opts: The number of resource groups in the subscription
The number of tags on the resource
The Azure region the resource is deployed in
questions.why: Cost depends on resource type, consumption, maintenance, geography (region), network traffic (egress), subscription type and Marketplace items. Tags and resource groups are free.

questions.q: Before deploying anything, you want to estimate the monthly cost of three VMs and a SQL database. Which tool?
questions.why: The pricing calculator estimates costs before you deploy. Cost Management analyzes and controls what you are already spending.

questions.q: You want an email when a subscription's spending reaches 80% of a monthly amount. What should you create?
opts: A budget in Microsoft Cost Management
questions.why: Budgets in Cost Management trigger alerts at thresholds you set. Budgets alert; they do not stop resources by themselves.

questions.q: Which TWO are uses of resource tags?
opts: Identifying which resources belong to a project
Grouping costs by department in cost reports
Preventing a resource from being deleted
questions.why: Tags are name/value pairs for organization, cost reporting, automation and governance. Locks prevent deletion.

questions.q: You need a browser-based shell with Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell already installed and signed in. What should you use?
questions.why: Cloud Shell runs in the browser (Bash or PowerShell) with the tools already installed and authenticated.

questions.q: You must manage on-premises servers and servers in AWS from the Azure portal, applying Azure Policy to them. What should you use?
questions.why: Azure Arc projects non-Azure resources (servers, Kubernetes, data services) into Azure Resource Manager so you can manage and govern them in Azure.

questions.q: What is infrastructure as code (IaC)?
opts: Defining infrastructure in files so it can be deployed the same way every time
Writing app code that runs on infrastructure
questions.why: IaC describes resources in code (ARM templates, Bicep) so deployments are repeatable and version-controlled.

questions.q: Which TWO are benefits of ARM templates?
opts: They replace the need for Azure RBAC
They are declarative: you say what you want, not how to build it
Deploying the same template again gives the same result
They only work from the Azure portal
questions.why: ARM templates are declarative JSON, repeatable (idempotent), orchestrated and modular. Bicep is a simpler language for the same deployments.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Every request to manage Azure resources, from the portal, CLI or PowerShell, goes through Azure Resource Manager.
Bicep is a language for declaring Azure resources that is simpler than ARM template JSON.
Azure Cloud Shell requires installing the Azure CLI on your own computer.
questions.why: ARM is the single management layer for all tools. Bicep compiles to ARM templates. Cloud Shell runs in the browser with the tools preinstalled.

questions.q: Which service gives personalized recommendations for reliability, security, performance, operational excellence and cost?
questions.why: Advisor analyzes your resources and recommends improvements in those five categories.

questions.q: Developers need to see request rates, response times and failure rates of their web app. Which feature?
questions.why: Application Insights, part of Azure Monitor, monitors the performance and usage of web applications.

questions.q: Where do you write queries (KQL) against logs collected by Azure Monitor?
questions.why: Log Analytics is the Azure Monitor tool for writing and running log queries.

questions.q: Match each need to the right tool.
rows: Is there an Azure outage in a region I use?
How can I cut costs on idle VMs?
Email me when CPU stays above 90%
Why is my web app slow for users?
questions.why: Service Health = Azure's health for you. Advisor = recommendations. Monitor alerts = act on your metrics and logs. Application Insights = app performance.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Azure status shows the health of Azure services globally.
Resource Health shows the health of your individual resources.
Azure Advisor can automatically fix every recommendation it makes.
questions.why: Service Health has three views: Azure status (global), Service Health (your services and regions) and Resource Health (your resources). Advisor recommends; you act.

questions.q: A web app is slow at peak hours. You add three more VMs behind the load balancer. What is this called?
questions.why: Adding more instances is horizontal scaling. Adding CPU or RAM to one VM is vertical scaling.

questions.q: You resize one VM from 4 GB to 16 GB of RAM. What is this called?
questions.why: Making one machine bigger is vertical. More machines is horizontal.

questions.q: In PaaS, which TWO are the cloud provider's responsibility?
questions.why: In PaaS, Microsoft runs the OS, hosts, network and datacenter. You always keep your data, accounts and access.

questions.q: Your developers want to build a custom app without configuring or patching servers. Which service model fits?
questions.why: PaaS gives you a managed platform to build on. SaaS is a finished app you just use. IaaS still leaves the OS to you.

questions.q: Which is an IaaS offering?
questions.why: VMs are IaaS: you manage the OS. Cosmos DB and App Service are PaaS. Microsoft 365 is SaaS.

questions.q: Match each service to its model.
rows: Azure Virtual Machines
Azure Cosmos DB
Microsoft 365
questions.why: You manage the OS only in IaaS. PaaS gives you a managed platform. SaaS is a finished app.

questions.q: Each Azure region pair is made of two regions in the same what?
questions.why: Pairs sit in the same geography (like US or Europe), usually at least 300 miles apart, so one disaster does not hit both.

questions.q: You have 30 subscriptions. You need to apply the same policies and access to all of them at once. What should you use?
questions.why: Management groups sit above subscriptions. Administrative units are an Entra feature for delegating admin of users and groups.

questions.q: You need to run a small piece of code when a file is uploaded, with no servers to manage. What should you use?
questions.why: Functions is serverless code: it runs on an event and bills per run. Container Instances runs a container you build.

questions.q: You need to report costs per department without moving any resources. What should you use?
questions.why: Tags add labels like Department=Finance that Cost Management can group by. Subscriptions would mean moving resources.

questions.q: Which TWO affect the cost of an Azure resource?
opts: Using ARM templates to deploy it
The region it is deployed in
questions.why: Prices differ by region, and data leaving Azure is billed. Resource groups and templates are free.

questions.q: You must make sure VMs can only be created in East US. What should you use?
questions.why: Allowed locations is a built-in policy. Locks only stop deletes or changes to resources that already exist.

questions.q: A dev team must only create VMs of approved sizes. What should you use?
questions.why: Allowed VM sizes is a built-in policy. Conditional Access controls sign-ins, not what gets deployed.

questions.q: Match each need to the right tool.
rows: Only allow VMs in one region
Stop anyone deleting a database
Let a user manage one resource group
Require MFA when signing in from outside
questions.why: Policy: what can be deployed. Locks: protect existing resources. RBAC: who can do what. Conditional Access: sign-in rules.

questions.q: What do you use to open Azure Cloud Shell?
questions.why: Cloud Shell runs in the browser, from the portal or shell.azure.com. It has Bash with Azure CLI and PowerShell.

questions.q: You want to be told when there are new recommendations to cut Azure costs. Which tool?
questions.why: Advisor makes the recommendations and can alert you when new ones appear.

questions.q: You need to be notified of an outage in an Azure region you use. Which tool?
questions.why: Service Health covers Azure's own issues: outages, planned maintenance and advisories in your regions.

questions.q: Where do you find planned maintenance for the Azure services you use?
questions.why: Planned maintenance is an Azure-side event, so it is in Service Health. Log Analytics queries your own logs.

sections.title: Cloud computing
sections.label: High
sections.note: Shared responsibility and cloud models appear on almost every attempt.
obj: public, private, hybrid and use cases
cold: **Cloud computing**: services (servers, storage, databases, networking, software) over the internet, on demand.
**Public**: provider-owned, shared hardware, no upfront hardware cost. **Private**: one organization, you manage hardware. **Hybrid**: both, workloads move between.

**Shared responsibility**: Microsoft always owns physical datacenter, network, hosts. You always own data, devices, accounts and identities. OS, network controls, applications and identity infrastructure vary by service type.
**CapEx** = upfront spend on hardware. **OpEx** = pay as you go. Consumption-based = pay only for what you use.
**Use cases:** public = variable load and test/dev; private = strict compliance or control; hybrid = sensitive data on-premises plus public capacity.

**Pricing models:** pay-as-you-go (flexible), Reservations and savings plans (commit 1 or 3 years, cheaper if steady), Spot (interruptible, lowest price). Azure Hybrid Benefit reuses existing licenses.
**Serverless**: you run code, the provider manages servers and scales automatically (Azure Functions).
traps: Which model buys hardware: private. Which is pay-as-you-go: public.
"Who patches the OS?" depends on IaaS (you) vs PaaS/SaaS (Microsoft).
Hybrid is not "multiple public clouds".
hooks: Public = shared. Private = yours. Hybrid = both.
CapEx = buy it. OpEx = rent it.

sections.title: Benefits of cloud services
sections.label: High
sections.note: Includes the SLA math you've missed in practice.
cold: **Scale up (vertical)** = bigger resource. **Scale out (horizontal)** = more instances.
**Scalability** = add or remove resources for load. **Elasticity** = do it automatically with demand.
**Reliability** = resiliency, redundancy, failover. **Predictability** = performance (autoscale, load balance, HA) and cost.
**Composite SLA = multiply** the SLAs; result is lower than any single one.
Downtime per year: 99% ≈ 3.65 days · 99.9% ≈ 8.76 hrs · 99.99% ≈ 52.6 min.
Management **of** the cloud (autoscale, templates, monitoring) vs management **in** the cloud (portal, CLI, PowerShell, APIs).
traps: Scalability vs elasticity (weak area).
Adding a component to a chain lowers the composite SLA.
hooks: Up = bigger box. Out = more boxes.
Composite SLA = multiply.

sections.title: Cloud service types
sections.label: High
sections.note: IaaS shared responsibility is a current weak area.
obj: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and their use cases.
cold: **IaaS**: rent VMs, storage, networks. You manage OS, apps, data. Lift and shift, test/dev.
**PaaS**: build and deploy apps without managing servers or OS. You manage app and data.
**SaaS**: finished software, usually subscription (Microsoft 365). You manage data and access.
Moving IaaS → PaaS → SaaS, Microsoft manages more.
traps: Azure VMs are IaaS: you patch the OS.
App Service, Functions are PaaS/serverless.
hooks: Moving right, Microsoft manages more.

sections.title: Core architectural components
sections.label: High
sections.note: 7 official objectives
sections.why: The first and most visible objective in Domain 2, and the hierarchy shows up again in Domain 3 (Policy, RBAC, locks, cost tags all apply at these scopes). Learn it once, use it everywhere.
obj: Azure regions, region pairs, sovereign regions
The hierarchy of resource groups, subscriptions and management groups
cold: Geography → region → availability zone → datacenter
Region pair = same geography, at least 300 miles apart; Brazil South is the one-way exception
Zonal vs zone-redundant vs non-regional services
Hierarchy: Tenant Root Group → management groups → subscriptions → resource groups → resources
Resource group rules: one group per resource, no nesting, no renaming, delete group = delete contents
Subscription = billing boundary + access control boundary
Management groups: 6 levels deep, 10,000 per directory, one parent
traps: Mixing up availability zones (inside a region) with region pairs (two regions)
Thinking a resource can be in two resource groups
Forgetting that group settings apply to current and future resources (module quiz miss)
hooks: Mom Sells Real Rugs = Management group, Subscription, Resource group, Resource
300 miles = a pair; zones are neighbors
A group is a box: trash the box, trash the contents

sections.title: Compute
sections.label: High
sections.note: 4 official objectives (compute half of 'compute and networking'
sections.why: Questions here are scenario-style: pick the right compute option for a described need. The control ladder (VMs → containers → App Service → Functions) also reinforces the IaaS/PaaS/serverless weak area.
obj: Compare compute types: containers, virtual machines, functions
VM options: Azure VMs, scale sets, availability sets, Azure Virtual Desktop
Application hosting: web apps, containers, virtual machines
cold: VMs are IaaS: you patch the OS
Scale set = identical VMs that auto scale; availability set = update and fault domains inside one region
VM name decoder: Standard_D2s_v5
Container Instances vs Container Apps vs AKS
Functions: event-driven, serverless, pay only while running; Durable Functions = stateful
App Service types: web apps, API apps, WebJobs, mobile apps
AI services (prebuilt) vs Machine Learning (custom) vs IoT
traps: Confusing scale sets (scale) with availability sets (resiliency)
Update domain (planned reboots) vs fault domain (shared power or network)
Picking a VM when the scenario says 'no infrastructure to manage'
hooks: Update = planned, Fault = failure
One container = ACI, smart scaling = Apps, a fleet = AKS
Event in, code runs, pay only while it runs

sections.title: Networking
sections.label: Medium-High
sections.note: 2 official objectives (virtual networking; public and private endpoints), but they cover a lot of ground
sections.why: Fewer objective lines than other sections, but each one is a service you must tell apart. The VPN vs ExpressRoute comparison is a classic exam question.
obj: Virtual networking: virtual networks, subnets, peering, Azure DNS, VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute
cold: VNet = private IP space split into subnets; NSGs filter, route tables and UDRs route
Peering joins VNets privately over the Microsoft backbone, even across regions
VPN Gateway: encrypted over the internet; site-to-site, point-to-site, network-to-network

sections.title: Cost management
sections.label: High
sections.note: You missed all three cost questions on practice test 1.
cold: **Six cost factors:** resource type, consumption, maintenance, geography, subscription type, Azure Marketplace.
**Billing zones** group regions for data-transfer pricing (not availability zones). Some inbound is free; outbound is priced by zone.
**Pricing calculator:** estimate before you deploy. Nothing is provisioned or charged. TCO calculator is retired.
**Cost Management:** cost analysis, cost alerts, budgets. Alerts: budget, credit (90% and 100%), department spending quota (EA). Budgets can trigger automation that suspends or changes resources.
**Tags:** name-value metadata for resource, cost, operations, security, governance and automation use. NOT inherited. Policy can require or reapply them.
**Pricing options:** pay-as-you-go (flexible), Reservations (stable, 1 or 3 years), savings plan for compute (hourly spend, flexible across compute), Spot (interruptible, can be evicted).
traps: Cost Management does not estimate before deployment. The pricing calculator does.
Tags do not flow down from resource groups.
Reservation is tied to specific resources; savings plan is tied to spend.

sections.title: Governance and compliance
sections.label: High
sections.note: ## Objectives
cold: **Purview:** data governance, risk and compliance. Automated discovery, sensitive-data classification, end-to-end lineage across on-premises, multicloud and SaaS.

**Azure Policy:** create, assign and manage rules that audit or enforce configuration (allowed regions, VM sizes, required tags). Inherited downward. Evaluates new and existing resources. Can remediate. Groups of policies are initiatives.
**Resource locks:** Delete and ReadOnly. Inherited. Apply regardless of RBAC. Remove the lock first to make a change.
**Service Trust Portal:** Microsoft's security, privacy and compliance documents and audit reports. Sign in with an Entra work or school account; NDA for some content.
traps: Policy controls what resources can be. RBAC controls what users can do. Locks stop accidental change or deletion.
An Owner is still blocked by a lock.
hooks: "Policy = rules. Lock = brake. RBAC = keys."

sections.label: High
sections.note: ## Objectives
obj: Azure Resource Manager and ARM templates (plus Bicep, IaC).
cold: **Portal:** web GUI; dashboards; resilient, presence in every datacenter.
**Cloud Shell:** browser-based, no install, already authenticated; choose PowerShell or CLI (Bash).
**PowerShell vs CLI:** equivalent; cmdlets vs Bash-style commands; both scriptable.
**Arc:** extends Azure management and governance to servers, Kubernetes, data services, SQL Server, VMs outside Azure, through ARM.

**ARM:** every request from any tool goes through it (authenticate, authorize, send to service). ARM templates are declarative JSON: repeatable, orchestrated, modular. Bicep is a simpler declarative language.
**Copilot in Azure:** AI assistant; validate its output.
traps: Arc manages non-Azure resources without migrating them. Advisor does not.
"Create a VM from a phone" means portal or Cloud Shell.
ARM is a management layer, not a tool you install.
hooks: "Everything goes through ARM."
"Arc brings outside things in."

sections.title: Monitoring tools
sections.label: High
sections.note: Advisor, Service Health and Monitor are easy to mix up.
obj: Azure Monitor (Log Analytics, alerts, Application Insights).
cold: **Advisor:** recommendations in five categories: Reliability, Security, Performance, Operational Excellence, Cost.
**Service Health:** Azure Status (global), Service Health (your services and regions: outages, planned maintenance, advisories), Resource Health (one resource).
**Monitor:** collects metrics and logs; Log Analytics = queries; Alerts = rule + action group (metric or log based); Application Insights = web app performance and usage. Drives autoscale.
Action groups are reusable across Monitor, Service Health and Advisor.
traps: Outage or planned maintenance → Service Health, not Advisor.
CPU over 80% alert → Monitor.
Recommendation to cut cost → Advisor.
hooks: "Advisor advises. Service Health warns. Monitor measures."

capex.learn: CapEx means paying upfront for hardware. The cloud's consumption model (pay-as-you-go) has no upfront cost.

spike.learn: Scalability (autoscale) adds resources when demand rises.

crash.learn: High availability keeps a second instance running. Without it, a crash takes a resource down.

patch.learn: With IaaS you patch the OS. PaaS and SaaS shift patching to Microsoft.

latency.learn: Geo-distribution puts apps in regional datacenters close to users.

breach.learn: Under shared responsibility, your data, devices, accounts and identities are always yours to protect.

residency.learn: Hybrid cloud keeps some data and workloads on-premises while using public cloud for the rest.

drift.learn: Governance in the cloud uses templates and policies to keep deployments compliant.

surprise.learn: Predictability comes from monitoring: you see problems before users do.

disaster.learn: Reliability means recovering from failures: backups, replication and disaster recovery.

zoneout.learn: A zone outage takes down one datacenter in a region. Spread resources across availability zones, or use zone-redundant services.

region.learn: If a whole region fails, a paired region or geo-redundant storage (GRS) keeps you running.

onprem.learn: VPN Gateway (encrypted, over the internet) or ExpressRoute (private, not over the internet) connects on-premises to Azure.

isolated.learn: Virtual network peering connects VNets directly over the Microsoft backbone.

exposed.learn: A private endpoint gives a service a private IP in your VNet, so it is not reachable from the internet.

dnsfail.learn: Azure DNS hosts your DNS domains and supports private zones. You buy domain names from a registrar.

storebill.learn: Access tiers: hot (frequent), cool (30 days), cold (90 days), archive (180 days, offline, cheapest to store).

bigmove.learn: Azure Data Box ships a physical device for moving large amounts of data when the network is too slow.

brute.learn: Multifactor authentication requires more than a password.

risky.learn: Conditional Access uses signals such as location and device to allow, block or require MFA.

hybridid.learn: Microsoft Entra Connect syncs on-premises Active Directory identities to Microsoft Entra ID.

meta.name: Microsoft Security, Compliance, and Identity Fundamentals

cards.front: Shared responsibility: what is ALWAYS the customer's job?
cards.back: Your **information and data**, your **devices** (PCs and mobile), and your **accounts and identities**. This holds for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.

cards.front: Shared responsibility: what is ALWAYS Microsoft's job in the cloud?
cards.back: The **physical datacenter**, the **physical network** and the **physical hosts**.

cards.front: Name the seven defense-in-depth layers, outside to inside.
cards.back: **Physical, Identity and access, Perimeter, Network, Compute, Application, Data.** Each layer slows an attacker if the one before it fails.
**Confidentiality** (only the right people see it), **Integrity** (it is not altered), **Availability** (it is there when needed).

cards.front: Zero Trust: the three guiding principles?
cards.back: **Verify explicitly** (always authenticate and authorize on all data points), **use least privilege access** (just-in-time, just-enough), **assume breach** (segment, encrypt, monitor).

cards.front: Zero Trust: the six foundational pillars?
cards.back: **Identities, Devices (endpoints), Applications, Data, Infrastructure, Networks.**
**Symmetric:** one key encrypts and decrypts. **Asymmetric:** a public and private key pair. What one key encrypts, only the other decrypts.

cards.front: Encryption at rest, in transit, in use?
cards.back: **At rest:** stored data (disk, database). **In transit:** moving over a network (HTTPS/TLS). **In use:** data being processed in memory.

cards.front: What is hashing, and how is it different from encryption?
cards.back: Hashing turns data into a **fixed-length value** and is **one-way**: you cannot reverse it. The same input always gives the same hash. Used to store passwords and check integrity. **Salting** adds a random value so identical passwords get different hashes.

cards.front: GRC: what do the three letters cover?
cards.back: **Governance:** the rules and processes that direct the organization. **Risk management:** identify, assess and respond to threats. **Compliance:** follow the laws and regulations that apply.
**Residency:** rules about the physical place data may be stored. **Sovereignty:** data is subject to the laws of the country or region where it is collected, held or processed.

cards.front: Why is identity called the primary security perimeter?
cards.back: Cloud apps, personal devices and remote work mean the corporate network is no longer the edge. **Who** is signing in (person, service or device) is what you can check everywhere.

cards.front: The four pillars of an identity infrastructure?
cards.back: **Administration** (create and manage identities), **Authentication** (prove who you are), **Authorization** (what you may do), **Auditing** (track who did what).
**Authentication (AuthN):** proving you are who you say you are. **Authorization (AuthZ):** deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed to access.

A service that **creates, stores and manages identities** and handles authentication, authorization and auditing for apps. With modern authentication the IdP issues a **security token** that apps trust. Microsoft Entra ID is one.
Sign in **once** and use that one credential to reach many apps and resources, without signing in again for each.

cards.front: What is a directory service? Name Microsoft's on-premises one.
cards.back: A hierarchical store of objects on a network (users, devices, groups). **Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)** is the on-premises one. It does not natively support mobile devices, SaaS apps or modern authentication.
A **trust relationship between identity providers** in different organizations or domains, so users sign in with their home identity. Trust is **not always two-way**.
Microsoft's **cloud-based identity and access management** service. Microsoft 365, Azure and Dynamics 365 tenants use it automatically. Formerly Azure Active Directory.

cards.front: The main identity types in Microsoft Entra ID?
cards.back: **Human** (workforce employees, and external guests, partners, customers), **workload** (applications, service principals, managed identities), **device**, and newer **agent identities** for AI agents.
The identity an **application** uses in a tenant, so it can be authenticated and given permissions. You must manage its credentials unless it is a managed identity.

cards.front: What is a managed identity? Two kinds?
cards.back: A service principal that **Azure manages for you**: no credentials to store or rotate. **System-assigned:** tied to one resource and deleted with it. **User-assigned:** standalone, can be shared by several resources.

cards.front: Device identity: registered vs joined vs hybrid joined?
cards.back: **Entra registered:** personal (BYOD) device, sign in with a personal or local account. **Entra joined:** organization-owned, sign in with a work account, cloud only. **Hybrid joined:** organization-owned, joined to on-premises AD and registered in Entra.

cards.front: What does Microsoft Entra External ID B2B collaboration do?
cards.back: Lets **guests** (partners, vendors) sign in with **their own identity** to use your apps. You manage their access, they manage their credentials.

cards.front: What is hybrid identity, and what makes it work?
cards.back: One identity for on-premises and cloud. **Microsoft Entra Connect Sync** or **Cloud Sync** synchronizes on-premises Active Directory with Microsoft Entra ID.

cards.front: Hybrid sign-in: password hash sync vs pass-through authentication vs federation?
cards.back: **Password hash sync:** a hash of the hash is stored in Entra, sign-in happens in the cloud, simplest. **Pass-through:** an on-premises agent validates the password, nothing stored in the cloud. **Federation:** Entra hands off to a separate trusted identity provider such as AD FS.

cards.front: What is multifactor authentication (MFA)? The three factor types?
cards.back: Sign-in that needs **two or more** of: something you **know** (password, PIN), something you **have** (phone, security key), something you **are** (fingerprint, face).

cards.front: Which authentication methods are passwordless in Microsoft Entra ID?
cards.back: **Windows Hello for Business**, **Microsoft Authenticator** (phone sign-in), and **passkeys (FIDO2)** security keys.

cards.front: Why is a Windows Hello PIN safer than a password?
cards.back: The PIN is **tied to that one device** and backed by its TPM chip. It is never sent to a server, so a stolen PIN is useless without the device.
Free, preconfigured baseline settings: **all users register for MFA**, **administrators must use MFA**, and **legacy authentication is blocked**. For organizations not using Conditional Access.
Users **change, reset or unlock** their own password with no help desk call, after proving identity with registered methods. Cuts help desk cost and downtime.

cards.front: Password protection: global vs custom banned password list?
cards.back: **Global:** maintained by Microsoft from real attack data, applied to everyone automatically. **Custom:** your own terms (brand, product names, locations). Both can also protect on-premises AD in a hybrid setup.

cards.front: Rank these by strength: password only, password + SMS, passwordless.
cards.back: Weakest: **password only**. Better: **password + second factor**. Best: **passwordless** (Windows Hello, Authenticator, passkey).

cards.front: Which methods can be used as a second factor in Entra MFA?
cards.back: Microsoft Authenticator, passkeys (FIDO2), Windows Hello for Business, OATH hardware or software tokens, SMS and voice call. A **password plus a security question is NOT MFA** in Entra sign-in.
Entra's policy engine: **if-then** rules that take **signals**, make a **decision**, and **enforce** it. Example: if a user signs in from outside the country, then require MFA.
**User or group**, **location** (IP range, country), **device** (platform, compliance), **application**, and **real-time sign-in or user risk** from ID Protection.

cards.front: Conditional Access: what decisions can it make?
cards.back: **Block access**, or **grant access**, optionally with requirements: MFA, a compliant device, a hybrid joined device, an approved app, or a password change.

cards.front: Microsoft Entra roles vs Azure roles (Azure RBAC)?
cards.back: **Entra roles** control access to **Entra resources**: users, groups, apps, licenses (for example Global Administrator, User Administrator). **Azure roles** control access to **Azure resources** such as VMs and storage (Owner, Contributor, Reader).
**Built-in:** fixed permission sets ready to use. **Custom:** you pick the permissions yourself, which needs a premium license. Always give the **least privileged** role that does the job.

Microsoft's **Security Service Edge (SSE)** solution: **Microsoft Entra Internet Access** (secure access to internet and SaaS) and **Microsoft Entra Private Access** (secure access to private apps without a VPN).

cards.front: At which scopes can an Azure role be assigned?
cards.back: **Management group, subscription, resource group, or a single resource.** Access is inherited downward.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Entra ID Governance for?
cards.back: Making sure the **right people have the right access to the right resources at the right time**. Covers the identity lifecycle (join, move, leave), access lifecycle and privileged access lifecycle.
Bundles the groups, apps and sites a role needs into an **access package**. Users request it, approval and **expiration** are built in. Works for guests too.
Scheduled checks where owners, managers or users themselves **confirm who still needs access** to groups, apps or roles. Access not confirmed can be removed automatically.

cards.front: What does Privileged Identity Management (PIM) do?
cards.back: Makes admin roles **just-in-time and time-bound**. Users are *eligible* and must **activate** the role, which can require **approval, MFA and a justification**. Everything is audited.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Entra ID Protection?
cards.back: Detects identity-based risks with Microsoft's threat signals, lets you **investigate** them in reports, and **remediates** automatically through risk-based Conditional Access.

cards.front: ID Protection: user risk vs sign-in risk?
cards.back: **Sign-in risk:** chance that this one sign-in is not the real owner (anonymous IP, atypical travel, password spray). **User risk:** chance that the identity itself is compromised (for example leaked credentials).

cards.front: How do you auto-remediate risk in ID Protection?
cards.back: Risk-based **Conditional Access**: medium or high **sign-in risk** requires MFA; high **user risk** requires a secure **password change**, or blocks access.

cards.front: What is a DDoS attack, and what does Azure DDoS Protection do?
cards.back: A flood of traffic meant to **exhaust an app's resources** so real users cannot reach it. Azure DDoS Protection detects and absorbs the attack at the Azure network edge.

cards.front: Azure DDoS Protection: the two paid tiers?
cards.back: **DDoS Network Protection** (covers a whole virtual network) and **DDoS IP Protection** (pay per protected public IP). Basic infrastructure protection for the Azure platform itself is on by default.

A **managed, cloud-based, stateful network firewall**. Usually placed in a central hub virtual network to control traffic for all your networks. Built-in high availability, scales automatically, and filters with network rules, application (FQDN) rules and threat intelligence.
Protects **web apps** from common exploits such as **SQL injection and cross-site scripting**. Works at layer 7. Runs on **Application Gateway, Azure Front Door** or Azure CDN.

cards.front: How do virtual networks give you segmentation?
cards.back: Each VNet is **isolated**: resources in different VNets cannot talk unless you connect them (peering). Inside a VNet you divide resources into **subnets**.

cards.front: What is a network security group (NSG)?
cards.back: A list of **allow and deny rules** that filters traffic to and from Azure resources in a VNet. Rules use **priority, source, destination, port and protocol**. Attached to a **subnet or a network interface**.

cards.front: NSG rules: how is priority processed?
cards.back: Lowest number first. The **first matching rule wins** and processing stops. Default rules (which you cannot delete) allow traffic inside the VNet and deny inbound from the internet.
A managed service that gives **RDP and SSH to VMs from the Azure portal over TLS**. The VMs need **no public IP address**, so RDP/SSH ports are not exposed to the internet.
A secure store for **secrets** (passwords, connection strings), **keys** (encryption keys) and **certificates**. Access is controlled with Microsoft Entra authentication and logged.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud?
cards.back: A **cloud-native application protection platform (CNAPP)**. Three pillars: **DevSecOps**, **cloud security posture management (CSPM)** and **cloud workload protection (CWPP)**. Covers Azure, AWS, GCP and on-premises.

cards.front: What is cloud security posture management (CSPM)?
cards.back: Continuously **assesses your resources for misconfigurations** and gives hardening **recommendations**. Shows the result as a **secure score**.

**Foundational CSPM is free:** recommendations, secure score, the Microsoft cloud security benchmark. **Defender CSPM is paid:** adds attack path analysis, cloud security explorer, agentless scanning and governance.

cards.front: What is the secure score in Defender for Cloud?
cards.back: One number that sums up your security posture from the recommendations. **Higher score means lower identified risk.** Fix recommendations and it goes up.

cards.front: What is the Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB)?
cards.back: Microsoft's set of **security best-practice controls** for Azure and other clouds. It is the **default standard** applied when you turn on Defender for Cloud.

cards.front: How do policies, standards and recommendations relate?
cards.back: A **security standard** (like MCSB or ISO 27001) is a set of rules built on **Azure Policy**. Resources are assessed against it. Each failed check becomes a **recommendation** telling you how to fix it.

cards.front: What does cloud workload protection add?
cards.back: Paid **Defender plans** per workload type (Servers, Containers, Storage, Databases, App Service, Key Vault and more). They detect threats and raise **security alerts**.
A Defender for Servers feature that keeps management ports (RDP, SSH) **closed** and opens them **only on request, for a limited time**, to approved IPs.

**SIEM:** collects and correlates logs from everywhere, raises alerts and incidents. **SOAR:** automates the response to those alerts with workflows. **XDR:** integrated detection and response across endpoints, identities, email and apps.
Microsoft's **cloud-native SIEM and SOAR** solution. Scales in the cloud, no servers to run.
**Collect** data at cloud scale, **Detect** threats with analytics and threat intelligence, **Investigate** incidents with AI and hunting, **Respond** rapidly with automation.
Built-in connections that **ingest data** from Microsoft services (Defender XDR, Entra ID, Microsoft 365), other clouds, and third-party products.
**Analytics rules** correlate data into alerts. Related alerts are grouped into **incidents** to investigate. **Hunting** lets analysts search proactively with queries (KQL) before any alert fires.
Automated response workflows built on **Azure Logic Apps**. Triggered by alerts or incidents through automation rules. This is the SOAR part.
Interactive dashboards that **visualize and monitor** the data you have connected.

cards.front: Where do you use Microsoft Sentinel today?
cards.back: In the **Microsoft Defender portal**, where SIEM and XDR are unified. Azure portal support for Sentinel ends after March 31, 2027.
A suite that **coordinates detection, prevention, investigation and response** across **endpoints, identities, email and applications**, and joins the signals into single incidents.

cards.front: What does Microsoft Defender for Office 365 protect?
cards.back: **Email and collaboration** (Exchange, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive) against **phishing, malicious links and attachments**. Includes Safe Links, Safe Attachments and attack simulation training.

cards.front: What does Microsoft Defender for Endpoint protect?
cards.back: **Devices**: laptops, phones, tablets, servers. Provides attack surface reduction, next-generation protection, **endpoint detection and response (EDR)** and automated investigation.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps?
cards.back: A **cloud access security broker (CASB)**. Discovers **shadow IT**, gives visibility and control over SaaS app use, and protects data in cloud apps.

cards.front: What does Microsoft Defender for Identity do?
cards.back: Uses **on-premises Active Directory signals** to detect compromised identities, lateral movement and insider actions.

cards.front: What is Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management?
cards.back: Continuous **asset discovery and vulnerability assessment** with **risk-based prioritization** and remediation tracking for devices and software.

Microsoft's threat research in the **Defender portal**: **threat actor profiles, indicators of compromise, threat articles and vulnerability data**, on the **Overview** and **Intel explorer** pages. It replaced the standalone Defender Threat Intelligence portal.

cards.front: What is the Microsoft Defender portal?
cards.back: **security.microsoft.com**. One place for incidents and alerts, advanced hunting, Microsoft Secure Score, threat intelligence, and Microsoft Sentinel.

cards.front: What is the Service Trust Portal?
cards.back: Microsoft's public site (**servicetrust.microsoft.com**) for **audit reports, certifications, compliance guides and security assessments** that show how Microsoft cloud services protect your data.

cards.front: What kinds of documents are on the Service Trust Portal?
cards.back: Independent **audit reports** (SOC, ISO, FedRAMP), **penetration test and security assessment** results, compliance guides and white papers.

cards.front: Service Trust Portal: what is My Library?
cards.back: A place to **save (pin) documents** you use often. You can be **notified when Microsoft updates them**.
**Control, Transparency, Security, Strong legal protections, No content-based targeting, Benefits to you.**
**Control:** you are in charge of your data, with easy tools and clear choices. **Transparency:** Microsoft is open about data collection and use so you can make informed decisions.
Microsoft does **not use your email, chat, files or other personal content to target advertising** to you.

cards.front: Privacy principles 'Strong legal protections' and 'Benefits to you'?
cards.back: **Strong legal protections:** Microsoft respects local privacy laws and fights for privacy as a human right. **Benefits to you:** when data is collected, it is used to benefit you and improve your experience.

cards.front: What is the Microsoft Purview portal?
cards.back: **purview.microsoft.com**. One place for Purview's **data security, data governance, and risk and compliance** solutions.

A Purview solution that helps you **assess and manage compliance** across your multicloud environment: prebuilt **assessments** for regulations, step-by-step **improvement actions**, and a **compliance score**.

cards.front: Compliance Manager: controls, assessments, regulations (templates), improvement actions?
cards.back: A **regulation** template (GDPR, ISO 27001) creates an **assessment**. The assessment is made of **controls**. Each control is met by **improvement actions** with guidance you carry out.
**Microsoft-managed** (Microsoft implements), **your controls** (customer-managed, you implement), **shared** (both).
A **risk-based** percentage showing progress on **improvement actions**. It helps you prioritize. It is **not a guarantee** of being compliant with a regulation.
**Compliance score:** Purview Compliance Manager, progress toward regulations and standards. **Secure score:** Microsoft Defender, strength of your security configuration.

cards.front: What does the default Compliance Manager assessment cover?
cards.back: The **data protection baseline**: key controls drawn from common regulations and standards, so every organization starts with an initial score.

cards.front: Microsoft Purview Information Protection: the four steps?
cards.back: **Know your data, protect your data, prevent data loss, govern your data.**

cards.front: Sensitive information types vs trainable classifiers?
cards.back: **Sensitive information types:** pattern-based (credit card, passport numbers). **Trainable classifiers:** AI that learns from examples to recognize kinds of content (resumes, source code, contracts).

**Content explorer:** a current snapshot of **which items** have a sensitivity label, retention label or sensitive info type, and where they are. **Activity explorer:** the **history of what was done** to labeled content (label changed, file copied to USB, printed).

cards.front: What is a sensitivity label? What can it do?
cards.back: A tag you apply to documents and emails. It is **customizable, stored as clear-text metadata, and persistent** (it travels with the content). It can **encrypt**, add **markings** (header, footer, watermark), and protect containers like Teams and sites. **One sensitivity label per item.**

cards.front: What is a sensitivity label policy?
cards.back: How labels are **published** to users and groups. Can set a **default label**, require **justification to lower** a label, and make **labeling mandatory**.
Policies that **detect and stop inappropriate sharing of sensitive information** across Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams and devices (Endpoint DLP). Actions: block, show a **policy tip**, alert.
**Retention policy:** the same settings for a whole location (site, mailbox). **Retention label:** set per item (document, email, folder). An item can have **only one retention label** at a time.
Declaring items as **records**: they get restrictions (cannot be deleted, edits limited), activities are logged, and at the end there is **disposition review** and proof of disposition.
**Retain only**, **delete only**, or **retain then delete**. Labels can be published for users to apply or applied automatically.
A Purview solution to **detect, investigate and act on risky activity by people inside** the organization: data theft by departing employees, data leaks, security policy violations.
**Policies** define risk indicators, **alerts** are raised, then **triage**, **investigate** in a case, and take **action** (reminder notice, or escalate).

cards.front: How does Insider Risk Management protect privacy?
cards.back: **Privacy by design:** usernames are **pseudonymized by default**, access is role-based, and investigator actions are audited.
Identifying and delivering **electronic information as evidence in legal cases**. Purview eDiscovery searches mailboxes, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive.

A **case** groups everything for one investigation. A **hold** preserves content so it cannot be deleted. **Search** finds content. **Export** delivers it. Premium features add review sets and analytics.
**On by default.** Records user and admin activity across Microsoft 365 in the unified audit log. Records are kept **180 days**.

Adds **longer retention** (one year by default for Entra ID, Exchange, SharePoint and OneDrive, **up to 10 years** with an add-on), **audit log retention policies**, and **intelligent insights** for investigations.
An **eDiscovery hold** preserves content tied to a legal **case**. A **retention policy** governs content lifetime for compliance generally.

questions.q: A company moves its email to a SaaS service. Which is still the company's responsibility?
opts: The accounts and identities used to sign in
Patching the mail server operating system
questions.why: Customers always keep responsibility for data, devices, and accounts and identities, even in SaaS.

questions.q: A file's contents were changed by an attacker without anyone noticing. Which part of the CIA triad was broken?
questions.why: Integrity means data is not altered without authorization. Confidentiality is about who can see it, availability about access when needed.

questions.q: Which Zero Trust principle is met by limiting admins to just-in-time and just-enough access?
questions.why: Least privilege limits access with JIT and JEA. Verify explicitly is about authenticating on all signals. Assume breach is about segmenting and monitoring.

questions.q: You need to store user passwords so that the original password cannot be recovered from the stored value. What should you use?
questions.why: Hashing is one-way. Encryption can be reversed with the key, so it does not meet the requirement.

questions.q: Which defense-in-depth layer do DDoS protection and firewalls at the edge of the network belong to?
questions.why: The perimeter layer guards against network-based attacks from outside, such as DDoS. The network layer is about segmentation inside.

questions.q: Which TWO are Zero Trust guiding principles?
questions.why: The three principles are verify explicitly, use least privilege access and assume breach. Zero Trust never trusts a network location by itself.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: In asymmetric encryption, data encrypted with the public key can be decrypted with the same public key.
A hash value can be decrypted to get the original data back.
HTTPS is an example of encryption in transit.
questions.why: Asymmetric encryption needs the other key of the pair. Hashing is one-way. HTTPS (TLS) protects data moving across a network.

questions.q: Match each example to the defense-in-depth layer.
rows: Badge access to the datacenter building
Multifactor authentication for sign-in
Patching virtual machine operating systems
Encrypting a database
questions.why: Physical is the building. Identity and access controls who signs in. Compute covers VMs and endpoints. Data is the innermost layer.

questions.q: A user enters a password and then approves a prompt on their phone. Which process is this?
questions.why: Proving who you are is authentication. Authorization happens afterwards and decides what you can access.

questions.q: After sign-in, a user can read a SharePoint site but cannot edit it. Which process decided that?
questions.why: Authorization sets the level of access an authenticated identity gets.

questions.q: Users at Contoso sign in to a partner's app with their Contoso accounts. The partner's identity provider trusts Contoso's. What is this called?
questions.why: Federation is a trust relationship between identity providers across organizations.

questions.q: Which statement about Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is true?
opts: It is an on-premises directory service that does not natively support SaaS apps and modern authentication
It replaces the need for any authentication
It is the cloud identity provider included with Microsoft 365
questions.why: AD DS is the on-premises directory. Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud identity provider built for modern authentication.

questions.q: With modern authentication, what does the identity provider give the client after a successful sign-in?
opts: An encryption key for the disk
questions.why: The identity provider issues a security token that the client presents to apps. Apps trust the token, not the password.

questions.q: Which TWO are pillars of an identity infrastructure?
questions.why: The four pillars are administration, authentication, authorization and auditing.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Authorization happens before authentication.
In a federation, trust between two identity providers is always bidirectional.
Single sign-on lets a user sign in once and access multiple applications.
questions.why: Authentication comes first. Federation trust can be one-way. SSO means one sign-in for many apps.

questions.q: An Azure VM needs to read secrets from Key Vault. You do not want to store or rotate any credentials. What should you use?
questions.why: Managed identities are managed by Azure, so there are no credentials in code or to rotate.

questions.q: A managed identity must be used by five different virtual machines and should exist independently of them. Which type fits?
questions.why: User-assigned identities are standalone and can be shared. System-assigned is tied to exactly one resource.

questions.q: An employee wants to use a personal phone for work email. Which device identity type fits a personal device?
questions.why: Registered is for personally owned (BYOD) devices. Joined and hybrid joined are for organization-owned devices.

questions.q: A company wants on-premises AD users to sign in to Microsoft 365 with the same password, and wants sign-in to keep working if the on-premises servers go down. Which method fits?
questions.why: With password hash sync, authentication happens in the cloud, so it does not depend on on-premises servers. Pass-through and federation both need on-premises components at sign-in.

questions.q: A vendor's staff must access your SharePoint site using their own company accounts. What should you use?
questions.why: B2B collaboration invites external users as guests who sign in with their own identity.

questions.q: Which TWO are workload identities?
questions.why: Workload identities are for software: applications, service principals and managed identities. Guests are human identities.

questions.q: Match each description to the identity type.
rows: An employee's work account
A partner invited as a guest
An app that authenticates to call an API
A company laptop joined to Entra
questions.why: Human identities are workforce or external. Workload identities are for software. Devices have their own identity.

questions.q: A user signs in with a password and a PIN they memorized. Is this multifactor authentication?
opts: Yes, a PIN is something you have
Yes, because two items were entered
No, both are something you know
questions.why: MFA needs factors from different categories. A password and a memorized PIN are both knowledge factors.

questions.q: Which sign-in method is passwordless?
opts: A FIDO2 passkey on a security key
A password plus a voice call
A password plus an SMS code
questions.why: Passkeys (FIDO2), Windows Hello for Business and Microsoft Authenticator phone sign-in remove the password.

questions.q: A small company has no Conditional Access licenses but wants MFA for all users and legacy authentication blocked. What should it turn on?
questions.why: Security defaults give a free baseline: MFA registration for all, MFA for admins, legacy authentication blocked.

sections.title: Security and compliance concepts
sections.label: High
sections.note: Small domain, but these ideas show up inside questions in every other domain. Two 3D models below.
cold: **Shared responsibility:** you always own **data, devices, accounts and identities**. Microsoft always owns the **physical datacenter, network and hosts**. The middle varies by IaaS, PaaS, SaaS.
**Defense in depth:** seven layers. Physical, identity and access, perimeter, network, compute, application, data.
**CIA triad:** confidentiality, integrity, availability.
**Zero Trust:** verify explicitly, use least privilege access, assume breach. Six pillars: identities, devices, applications, data, infrastructure, networks.
**Encryption:** symmetric = one key, asymmetric = public/private pair. At rest, in transit, in use.
**Hashing:** one-way, fixed length, same input gives same output. Used for passwords, with a salt.
**GRC:** governance (rules), risk management (identify and respond), compliance (follow laws). **Residency** = where data is stored. **Sovereignty** = whose laws apply.
traps: Hashing is not encryption. It cannot be reversed.
'Trust the internal network' is never a Zero Trust answer.
Perimeter (DDoS, edge firewall) vs network (segmentation inside).
hooks: Never trust, always verify.
Know, Have, Are is MFA. Verify, Least, Assume is Zero Trust.

sections.title: Identity concepts
sections.label: Medium
sections.note: Authentication vs authorization is the most common pair on the exam.
obj: Identity as the primary security perimeter
cold: **Identity is the new perimeter** because apps, devices and people are outside the corporate network.
**Four pillars:** administration, authentication, authorization, auditing.
**AuthN** = who are you. **AuthZ** = what may you do.
**Identity provider:** issues security tokens that apps trust. Enables **single sign-on**.
**AD DS** = on-premises directory. **Microsoft Entra ID** = cloud identity provider.
**Federation:** trust between identity providers of different organizations. Not always two-way.
traps: Authentication always comes before authorization.
AD DS is not Entra ID.
hooks: AuthN = who. AuthZ = what.

sections.title: Microsoft Entra ID and identity types
sections.label: High
sections.note: Know each identity type and the three hybrid sign-in methods.
obj: types of identities, including workload identities
cold: **Microsoft Entra ID:** cloud identity and access management. Every Microsoft 365 and Azure tenant has one.
**Identity types:** human (workforce, external), workload (apps, service principals, managed identities), device, and agent identities for AI.
**Managed identity:** Azure manages the credentials. System-assigned = one resource. User-assigned = shared, standalone.
**Devices:** registered (personal), joined (company, cloud), hybrid joined (company, on-premises AD plus Entra).
**External ID B2B:** guests sign in with their own identity.
**Hybrid identity:** Entra Connect Sync or Cloud Sync. Sign-in by password hash sync, pass-through authentication, or federation.
traps: Registered = personal device. Joined = company device.
Password hash sync still works if on-premises is down. Pass-through does not.
Guest users are human identities, not workload identities.
hooks: No secrets in code: managed identity.

**Passwordless:** Windows Hello for Business, Microsoft Authenticator, passkeys (FIDO2).
**Security defaults:** free baseline. MFA registration for all, MFA for admins, legacy authentication blocked.
**SSPR:** users reset their own passwords. Fewer help desk calls.
**Password protection:** global banned list (Microsoft, automatic) and custom banned list (your terms). Works for on-premises AD too.
traps: Password plus PIN is not MFA: both are 'know'.
Security questions are for SSPR only, not for sign-in MFA.
A Windows Hello PIN never leaves the device.
hooks: Know, Have, Are.

**Entra roles** manage Entra resources (users, groups, apps). **Azure roles** manage Azure resources (VMs, storage).
**Built-in** roles are ready-made. **Custom** roles need a premium license.
**Least privilege:** the smallest role that does the job.
**Global Secure Access:** Entra Internet Access and Entra Private Access (Security Service Edge).
traps: Global Administrator is an Entra role. Owner is an Azure role.
Security defaults and Conditional Access are not used together.
hooks: Conditional Access = if this, then that.

sections.title: Identity protection and governance
sections.label: High
sections.note: Four tools that get mixed up: ID Governance, access reviews, PIM, ID Protection.
cold: **ID Governance:** right people, right access, right resources, right time. Entitlement management uses **access packages**.
**Access reviews:** regularly confirm who still needs access. Remove what is not confirmed.
**PIM:** just-in-time, time-bound, approval-based activation of privileged roles.
**ID Protection:** detects **user risk** (identity compromised) and **sign-in risk** (this sign-in is suspicious). Remediates with risk-based Conditional Access.
traps: Leaked credentials = user risk. Anonymous IP or atypical travel = sign-in risk.
PIM activates roles. Access reviews recertify them.
hooks: PIM = admin only when needed.

sections.title: Core infrastructure security in Azure
sections.label: High
sections.note: Overlaps with AZ-900 Domain 2. Know which service does which job.
obj: network segmentation with Azure virtual networks
cold: **DDoS Protection:** keeps apps available during traffic floods. Network Protection (per VNet) or IP Protection (per public IP).
**Azure Firewall:** managed, stateful, central firewall. Filters by IP, port and FQDN.
**WAF:** protects web apps from SQL injection and cross-site scripting. On Application Gateway or Front Door.
**VNets** isolate. **Subnets** segment inside a VNet.
**NSG:** allow and deny rules by priority on a subnet or network interface.
**Bastion:** RDP and SSH from the portal over TLS. No public IP on the VM.
**Key Vault:** secrets, keys, certificates.
traps: NSG cannot filter by domain name. Azure Firewall can.
WAF is for web apps (layer 7). Azure Firewall is for network traffic.
Just-in-time VM access is Defender for Cloud, not Bastion.
hooks: Bastion = the safe gate to your VMs.

**eDiscovery:** find, hold and export content as legal evidence.
**Audit (Standard):** on by default, 180 days.
**Audit (Premium):** one year by default for core services, up to 10 years with an add-on, retention policies.
traps: eDiscovery hold is for a legal case. Retention policy is general.
Audit answers 'who did what, when'.
hooks: Insider = people. eDiscovery = evidence. Audit = activity.
