domains.3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

cards.back: **Security group:** grants access to resources (Azure roles, apps, licenses). Members can be users, devices, service principals and other groups. **Microsoft 365 group:** collaboration (shared mailbox, calendar, SharePoint, Teams). Members are users only.

**Assigned:** an admin adds and removes members by hand. **Dynamic user / dynamic device:** a rule on attributes (for example `user.department -eq "Sales"`) adds and removes members automatically. Dynamic groups need **Microsoft Entra ID P1**, and you **cannot add members by hand**.

cards.front: How do you create many users at once?
cards.back: **Bulk create** in the Entra admin center: download the CSV template, fill it, upload it. PowerShell (Microsoft Graph) and the Graph API also work.

cards.front: What must be set on a user before you assign a license?
cards.back: The **usage location** (country). Some services are not available in every country, so a license cannot be assigned without it.

cards.front: Group-based licensing: what is it and what does it need?
cards.back: Assign a license to a **group** and every member gets it; members who leave lose it. Needs a paid Entra plan such as **P1** (or Microsoft 365 E3/Business Premium). Errors show per user, for example when no licenses are left.

You **invite** them with their own email. They sign in with **their own** identity (work account, Microsoft account, Google, one-time passcode). They appear as **UserType: Guest** and get access you grant, like any other user.

cards.front: SSPR: what license does password reset need, and who can configure it?
cards.back: Self-service password **reset** needs **Microsoft Entra ID P1** (password *change* is free for cloud users). Writeback to on-premises needs P1/P2. Configure it as an **Authentication Policy Administrator**, scoped to **None, Selected (one group), or All**.
Admin accounts are **always enabled** for SSPR and **always need two methods** (a two-gate policy). You cannot turn that off for admins with the SSPR scope setting.

cards.front: What happens to a deleted user?
cards.back: It goes to **Deleted users** and can be **restored for 30 days** with its group memberships and licenses. After 30 days it is permanently deleted.

cards.front: The four fundamental Azure built-in roles?
cards.back: **Owner:** full access, including assigning roles. **Contributor:** full access to manage resources, **cannot assign roles**. **Reader:** view only. **User Access Administrator:** manage user access (role assignments) only.
Can **assign roles** (and can be limited with conditions to certain roles or principals), but cannot manage the resources themselves. A least-privilege alternative to Owner for delegating access.

cards.front: The four Azure RBAC scopes, top to bottom?
cards.back: **Management group → Subscription → Resource group → Resource.** A role assigned at a scope is **inherited** by everything below it.

cards.front: What makes up a role assignment?
cards.back: **Security principal** (user, group, service principal, managed identity) + **role definition** (what actions) + **scope** (where).

cards.front: How do multiple role assignments combine?
cards.back: **Additively.** Effective permissions are the union of all assignments. Reader at the subscription plus Contributor on one resource group = Contributor on that group, Reader everywhere else. **Deny assignments** win over allows.

cards.front: Actions vs DataActions in a role definition?
cards.back: **Actions** = management plane (create, delete, configure). **DataActions** = data plane (read blob contents, send queue messages). Owner does **not** automatically read blob data through Entra auth; you need roles such as **Storage Blob Data Reader**.

cards.front: Azure roles vs Microsoft Entra roles?
cards.back: **Azure roles** control Azure resources (VMs, storage, networks) at management group to resource scope. **Entra roles** control directory objects (users, groups, apps), for example Global Administrator or User Administrator. A Global Administrator can **elevate** to User Access Administrator at root scope.

cards.front: Virtual Machine Contributor can do what?
cards.back: Manage **virtual machines**, but **not** sign in to them and **not** manage the virtual network or storage account they connect to.

cards.front: How do you check what someone can do?
cards.back: Resource → **Access control (IAM)** → **Check access**, or the **Role assignments** tab. It shows direct and **inherited** assignments and the scope each came from.
**RBAC:** *who* can do *what* actions. **Policy:** *what* resources may look like, whoever creates them (allowed regions, required tags, allowed SKUs). Policy can deny even an Owner.

**Deny** (block the request), **Audit** (log non-compliance), **Append** / **Modify** (add or change properties such as tags), **AuditIfNotExists** / **DeployIfNotExists** (check or deploy a related resource), **Disabled**.

cards.front: Policy definition vs initiative vs assignment?
cards.back: **Definition:** one rule. **Initiative:** a group of definitions managed together. **Assignment:** applies a definition or initiative to a scope, with optional **exclusions** and parameters.

cards.front: What happens to existing resources when you assign a Deny policy?
cards.back: They are **not deleted or changed**. They show as **non-compliant**. Fix them with a **remediation task** (for Modify and DeployIfNotExists, which use a **managed identity**) or by hand.
**CanNotDelete (Delete):** can read and modify, cannot delete. **ReadOnly:** can read, cannot modify or delete. Locks are **inherited** by child resources and apply to **everyone, including Owners**.

cards.front: Who can create or remove locks?
cards.back: Anyone with `Microsoft.Authorization/locks/*`: **Owner** and **User Access Administrator** among built-in roles. Contributor cannot.

**No.** A tag on a resource group or subscription is **not** applied to the resources in it. Use Azure Policy (for example *Inherit a tag from the resource group*, a **Modify** policy) to copy tags. Up to **50 tags** per resource.

A resource is in **exactly one** resource group. The group has a location for its **metadata**, but its resources can be in **any region**. Deleting a group **deletes everything in it**. Resource groups cannot be nested.

Organize subscriptions for policy and RBAC. A **root management group** per tenant. Up to **six levels** of depth below root (not counting the subscription level). Each subscription and management group has **one parent**.

cards.front: Budgets vs cost alerts vs Advisor?
cards.back: **Budget:** a spending limit with alert thresholds (actual or forecasted). It **does not stop resources** by itself; it can trigger an **action group**. **Cost alerts:** budget, credit and quota alerts, plus anomaly alerts. **Azure Advisor:** recommendations such as resizing or shutting down underused VMs and buying reservations.

cards.front: Storage firewall: default action and options?
cards.back: Set public network access to **Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses**. Allow **VNet subnets** (needs a **Microsoft.Storage service endpoint**), **public IP ranges** (not private RFC 1918 addresses), **resource instances**, and **trusted Microsoft services** as an exception.

Two keys, **key1 and key2**, each gives **full access** to the account. Rotate one while apps use the other. Store them in **Key Vault**. You can **disallow Shared Key** authorization to force Entra ID.

**User delegation SAS:** signed with **Microsoft Entra** credentials; Blob and Data Lake only; **recommended**. **Service SAS:** signed with the **account key**, one service. **Account SAS:** signed with the account key, **one or more services**, plus service-level operations.

cards.front: What is in a SAS token?
cards.back: Signed fields such as **sp** (permissions), **st/se** (start and expiry), **sip** (allowed IPs), **spr** (HTTPS only), **sr** (resource) and the **sig** signature. Anyone holding the URL has that access until it expires.

Defined on a **container, file share, queue or table**. A **service SAS** can reference it for start, expiry and permissions. **Max five per container.** Revoke every SAS that uses it by **deleting or changing the policy**, without rotating keys.

cards.front: How do you revoke an ad hoc service SAS with no stored access policy?
cards.back: **Regenerate the account key** that signed it (or wait for expiry). That breaks every SAS and app using that key.

cards.front: Azure Files identity-based access: the three identity sources?
cards.back: **On-premises AD DS** (hybrid users synced to Entra), **Microsoft Entra Domain Services**, **Microsoft Entra Kerberos** (no line of sight to a domain controller needed). **One source per storage account.** Kerberos must be enabled in SMB security settings.

cards.front: Share-level vs file-level permissions in Azure Files?
cards.back: **Share level:** Azure RBAC roles such as **Storage File Data SMB Share Reader / Contributor / Elevated Contributor**, or a **default share-level permission** for all authenticated users. **Directory and file level:** Windows **NTFS ACLs**. Both must allow access.

cards.front: Azure Files over SMB: which port must be open?
cards.back: **TCP 445** outbound. Many ISPs block it; use VPN, ExpressRoute or Azure File Sync if so.
**Standard general-purpose v2** (blobs, files, queues, tables; most uses). **Premium block blobs**, **Premium file shares**, **Premium page blobs** (SSD, low latency, one service each).

**LRS:** 3 copies in one datacenter. **ZRS:** 3 copies across **availability zones**. **GRS:** LRS plus an async copy (LRS) in the **paired region**. **GZRS:** ZRS plus a copy in the paired region. Add **RA-** for **read access** to the secondary.
LRS: a rack or drive. **ZRS:** a whole **zone** (datacenter). **GRS/GZRS:** a whole **region**. **RA-GRS/RA-GZRS:** read from the secondary **without** waiting for failover.
Premium accounts support **LRS and ZRS** only. No geo-redundancy.

cards.front: What can't you change after creating a storage account?
cards.back: The **name** (globally unique, 3-24 lowercase letters and numbers) and the **region**. The **performance tier** (Standard vs Premium) also cannot be changed. Redundancy can be changed, sometimes needing a conversion.

Copies **block blobs** asynchronously between accounts. Needs **versioning on both** accounts and **change feed on the source**. GPv2 or premium block blob. Not with **hierarchical namespace**. **Snapshots are not replicated.** Archive tier blobs break replication.

**Always on**, AES-256, cannot be disabled. Keys: **Microsoft-managed** (default) or **customer-managed** in **Key Vault** or Managed HSM (the vault needs **soft delete and purge protection**). **Infrastructure encryption** (double) must be chosen **at creation**. **Encryption scopes** use different keys per container or blob.

**AzCopy:** command line for fast copy and **sync** to and from blobs and files (`azcopy copy`, `azcopy sync`), auth with Entra or SAS. **Storage Explorer:** desktop GUI to browse and manage blobs, files, queues and tables.
Turns blob storage into **Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2**: real directories and POSIX ACLs for analytics. Some blob features (for example object replication) are not supported with it.
Fully managed **SMB** (port 445) or **NFS** (premium only) shares. Set a **quota** (size). Mount from Windows, Linux or macOS. **Azure File Sync** caches shares on Windows Servers.

**Storage Sync Service** → **sync group** → one **cloud endpoint** (the Azure file share) + **server endpoints** (folders on registered servers). **Cloud tiering** keeps hot files local and leaves cold files as pointers.

cards.front: Share snapshots and soft delete for Azure Files?
cards.back: **Share snapshots:** read-only, point-in-time copies of the **whole share**; restore single files from them. **Soft delete:** keeps a **deleted share** for **1-365 days** so you can undelete it. Deleting a share deletes its snapshots too.

**Private** (no anonymous access), **Blob** (anonymous read of blobs only), **Container** (anonymous read and list). Anonymous access must also be **allowed at the account level**, which is off by default for new accounts.

**Hot** (frequent access), **Cool** (30 days), **Cold** (90 days), **Archive** (180 days, **offline**). Deleting or moving earlier than the minimum charges an **early deletion** fee. Hot or Cool can be the account default; Archive is set **per blob**.

cards.front: How do you read an archived blob?
cards.back: **Rehydrate** it: change its tier to Hot, Cool or Cold, or **copy** it to an online tier. **Standard priority** can take up to **15 hours**; **High priority** usually under **1 hour**.

Rules (JSON) per account that **move blobs to cooler tiers** or **delete** them after N days since **last modification**, **creation** or **last access** (needs access tracking). Filter by **prefix** or blob index tag. Also manages **versions** and **snapshots**. Runs about once a day.

cards.front: Blob versioning vs blob soft delete vs snapshots?
cards.back: **Versioning:** every overwrite keeps the **previous version** automatically. **Soft delete:** deleted blobs are kept for a retention period (1-365 days). **Snapshots:** read-only copies you take **by hand**. **Point-in-time restore** needs versioning, change feed and soft delete.
WORM: **time-based retention** (cannot modify or delete for N days) and **legal hold** (until cleared). Set at container or version level. For regulatory records.
**$schema**, **contentVersion**, **parameters** (values at deploy time), **variables** (computed values), **functions**, **resources** (required), **outputs** (values returned).
`param` (inputs), `var` (computed values), `resource` (symbolic name + type@apiVersion), `module` (another Bicep file), `output`. Bicep **compiles to an ARM JSON template**; no state file.

cards.front: Convert between Bicep and ARM JSON?
cards.back: `az bicep build` turns **Bicep into JSON**. `az bicep decompile` turns **JSON into Bicep** (best effort, review the result).

cards.front: How do you export a template from what already exists?
cards.back: Resource group or resource → **Export template** (current state), or **Deployments** history → a deployment's template (what was deployed). Exports may need cleanup and parameterizing.

**Incremental (default):** adds and updates resources in the template, **leaves others alone**. **Complete:** also **deletes** resources in the resource group that are **not in the template**. Use **what-if** to preview.

cards.front: Commands to deploy a template to a resource group?
cards.back: CLI: `az deployment group create -g RG1 --template-file main.bicep --parameters @params.json`. PowerShell: `New-AzResourceGroupDeployment`. Other scopes: `az deployment sub/mg/tenant create`.
Makes Resource Manager deploy one resource **after** another (for example a NIC before the VM). Bicep usually adds it **automatically** when you reference another resource's symbolic name.
`resourceGroup().location`, `uniqueString()` (deterministic hash for unique names), `concat()` / string interpolation in Bicep, `resourceId()`, `parameters()` and `variables()` in JSON.

A **parameters file** (`.parameters.json` or `.bicepparam`) supplies values per environment. Mark passwords `securestring` / `@secure()` and pull them from **Key Vault** with a reference, not plain text.
**B** burstable (cheap, low steady use), **D** general purpose, **E** memory optimized, **F** compute optimized, **L** storage optimized, **N** GPU, **M** very large memory.
Pick a new size; the VM **restarts**. If the size is **not available** on the current hardware cluster, you must **deallocate (stop)** the VM first to see and choose it.
**OS disk** (boot, persistent), **temporary disk** (local, **data lost** on deallocate, redeploy or host move; D: on Windows), **data disks** (persistent, attach several).

cards.front: Managed disk types, fast to slow?
cards.back: **Ultra Disk** and **Premium SSD v2** (data disks only, adjustable IOPS), **Premium SSD** (production), **Standard SSD** (light use), **Standard HDD** (backup, dev). You can **grow** a disk but **not shrink** it.

Spreads VMs across **fault domains** (shared power and network, **max 3**) and **update domains** (rebooted together, **max 20**, default 5). Set at VM creation. **99.95%** SLA for 2+ VMs. Protects against rack failure, not datacenter failure.
Separate datacenters with independent power, cooling and network in one region. VMs in **2+ zones** get a **99.99%** SLA. You cannot use an availability set and a zone for the same VM.

cards.front: VM Scale Sets: Flexible vs Uniform?
cards.back: **Flexible (recommended):** mix VM sizes, up to 1000 VMs, full VM control, spread across zones and fault domains. **Uniform:** identical VMs from one model. Orchestration mode is **fixed at creation**.

**Minimum, maximum and default** instance counts. **Scale-out** and **scale-in** rules on metrics (for example CPU over 70% for 10 min), a **cooldown**, or schedules. **Scale-in policy** decides which VM is removed first.

**Server-side encryption** is always on. **Encryption at host** also encrypts temp disks and caches end to end; **use it for new VMs**. **Azure Disk Encryption** (BitLocker/DM-Crypt with Key Vault) is **retiring on 15 Sept 2028**; migrate to encryption at host.

**Another resource group or subscription:** Move (with its disks, NIC, IP and other dependencies); the VM's **resource ID changes**, its region does not. **Another region:** **Azure Resource Mover** (uses Site Recovery replication) or Site Recovery directly.
**Basic** (learning, small), **Standard** (more storage and throughput), **Premium** (adds **geo-replication**, **private endpoints**, content trust, more throughput). All are private registries.

cards.front: How should apps pull images from ACR?
cards.back: With a **managed identity** or service principal that has the **AcrPull** role. The **admin user** is **disabled by default** and is for testing only.

cards.front: Build an image in Azure without Docker locally?
cards.back: `az acr build --registry myreg --image app:v1 .` uses **ACR Tasks** to build in the cloud and push to the registry.

Run containers **without managing servers or orchestration**. Billed per second. Good for simple apps, tasks and burst jobs. A **container group** is containers that share host, network, storage and lifecycle (like a pod). Multi-container groups are **Linux only**.

Set **CPU and memory** per container at deploy time; to change them you **redeploy**. ACI has **no built-in autoscale**: run more container groups yourself. Restart policy: **Always, OnFailure, Never**.

Serverless containers for microservices and APIs on a managed Kubernetes base. **KEDA** autoscaling (HTTP, TCP, CPU, memory, queues and events), **scale to zero**, **revisions** with traffic splitting, ingress, Dapr. You don't manage the cluster.

**Min and max replicas** per revision. **HTTP rule:** add a replica when concurrent requests per replica pass the threshold (default 10). Min replicas 0 = **scale to zero** (no usage charge while idle). **Vertical scaling is not supported.**

A revision is an **immutable snapshot** of the app. Changing **scale rules** or the container creates a new revision. In **multiple revision mode** you split traffic between revisions (blue-green, canary).

cards.front: ACI vs Container Apps vs AKS?
cards.back: **ACI:** one-off or simple containers, no autoscale. **Container Apps:** serverless microservices with autoscale and scale to zero. **AKS:** full Kubernetes control, you manage more.

cards.front: What does an App Service plan define?
cards.back: The **region**, **OS** (Windows or Linux), **pricing tier** (features) and **instance size and count**. **All apps in the plan share** those instances, and scale settings apply to **every app in the plan**.

cards.front: App Service tiers in one line each?
cards.back: **Free/Shared:** shared VMs, dev only. **Basic:** dedicated, manual scale, custom domains and TLS. **Standard:** autoscale, **deployment slots**, backups. **Premium v3:** more scale and power. **Isolated v2:** dedicated **network isolation** (App Service Environment).
**Basic 3**, **Standard 10**, **Premium 30**, **Isolated 100**. Autoscale rules start at **Standard**.
Add a **CNAME** (subdomain) or **A record** (root) pointing to the app, plus a **TXT record `asuid`** to prove ownership. Needs a **paid tier** (not Free).

**App Service managed certificate** (free, auto-renew, **not wildcard**), import from **Key Vault**, or upload a **PFX**. Bind with **SNI SSL** or IP SSL. Turn on **HTTPS Only** and set **minimum TLS 1.2**. TLS binding needs **Basic or higher**.
Backs up **app content, configuration and a linked database**. Custom backups need **Basic or higher**. **Basic:** production slot only. Standard and up: more slots and higher limits.

cards.front: App Service networking: inbound vs outbound?
cards.back: **Inbound:** **access restrictions** (allow/deny by IP, service tag, VNet) and **private endpoints** (private IP). **Outbound:** **VNet integration** lets the app reach resources in a VNet; **Hybrid Connections** reach on-premises endpoints.

Live apps with their own host names (staging, test) in **Standard or higher** (Standard has 5). **Swap** warms up the target instances first, so **no downtime**. **Swap back** to roll back. **Slot settings (sticky)** stay with the slot. Route a percentage of traffic to a slot to test in production.

cards.front: Scale up vs scale out for App Service?
cards.back: **Scale up:** bigger tier or instance size (more CPU, memory, features). **Scale out:** more instances, manual or **autoscale** rules (Standard+), or **automatic scaling** in Premium.

cards.front: How many IPs does Azure reserve in each subnet?
cards.back: **Five:** the network address, the **first three** host addresses (gateway and Azure DNS) and the **broadcast** (last) address. A /24 gives **251** usable addresses. The smallest IPv4 subnet is **/29** (3 usable).
Use private ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16). **Peered or connected VNets must not overlap.** You can **add** address ranges to a VNet later. A subnet in use cannot be resized past its resources.

Connects two VNets over the **Microsoft backbone** with private IPs, low latency. **Regional or global** (cross-region). **Not transitive**: A↔B and B↔C does not give A↔C. Needs **Network Contributor** (or equivalent) on both sides. Address spaces must not overlap.

The **hub** peering sets **Allow gateway transit**; the **spoke** peering sets **Use remote gateways**. The spoke then uses the hub's VPN/ExpressRoute gateway. A spoke that **has its own gateway** cannot use remote gateways.

**Standard:** always **static**, **secure by default** (closed until an NSG allows), zone-redundant or zonal, works with Standard Load Balancer. **Basic:** static or dynamic, open by default, **retired**. Dynamic IPs can change on deallocation.

A **route table** with routes (prefix → next hop), **associated to subnets**. Next hop types: **Virtual appliance** (an NVA IP), **Virtual network gateway** (VPN), **Virtual network**, **Internet**, **None** (drop).

cards.front: How does Azure pick a route?
cards.back: **Longest prefix match** first. If prefixes tie: **UDR** beats **BGP** beats **system** routes. A UDR can override system routes, including peering routes.

Peering isn't transitive, so add **UDRs** in each spoke sending the other spoke's range to an **NVA or Azure Firewall** in the hub (with IP forwarding on), or use **Azure Virtual Network Manager** / Virtual WAN.

**Effective routes** on a NIC, Network Watcher **Next hop** (which route wins), **IP flow verify** (which NSG rule allows or denies), **Connection troubleshoot** (end-to-end test), **Effective security rules**.

By **priority, 100 to 4096**, **lowest number first**. The **first match wins** and processing stops. Rules match on source, destination, port, protocol (5-tuple). NSGs are **stateful**: return traffic is allowed.

**Inbound:** 65000 AllowVNetInBound, 65001 AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound, **65500 DenyAllInbound**. **Outbound:** 65000 AllowVnetOutBound, 65001 AllowInternetOutBound, 65500 DenyAllOutBound. You **cannot delete** them, only override with lower numbers.

cards.front: NSG on both the subnet and the NIC?
cards.back: **Inbound:** subnet NSG first, then NIC NSG. **Outbound:** NIC NSG first, then subnet NSG. Traffic must be **allowed by both**. Check the result with **Effective security rules** or **IP flow verify**.
Group **NICs by role** (WebServers, DbServers) and use the ASG as source or destination in NSG rules instead of IP addresses. All NICs in an ASG must be in the **same VNet**.

Named groups of Microsoft IP prefixes kept up to date by Azure, for NSG rules: **Internet, VirtualNetwork, AzureLoadBalancer, Storage, Sql, AzureCloud**, and regional versions like **Storage.WestEurope**.

**Developer:** free, shared, one connection, no subnet. **Basic:** dedicated, 2 instances. **Standard:** native client, shareable links, IP-based connect, custom ports, file transfer, scaling 2-50. **Premium:** session recording, private-only. You can **upgrade, not downgrade**.

A subnet named exactly **AzureBastionSubnet**, **/26 or larger**, and a **Standard static public IP** (except Premium private-only). Users connect over **TLS 443** from the portal; target VMs need **no public IP**. Peered VNets are reachable (not with Developer).

Enabled **per subnet per service** (Microsoft.Storage, Microsoft.Sql…). Traffic to that service goes over the **Azure backbone** with the subnet's identity, so the PaaS firewall can allow the subnet. The service **keeps its public IP**. Free. Not reachable from on-premises.

A **NIC with a private IP** from your VNet mapped to **one specific resource** (a storage account's blob service, a SQL server). Reachable from **peered VNets and on-premises** (VPN/ExpressRoute). Needs **private DNS** (for example `privatelink.blob.core.windows.net`). Billed per hour and per GB.

Host your domain's records in Azure. **Delegate** by setting the four Azure **NS records** at your registrar. Azure DNS does **not** sell domains. Records: A, AAAA, **CNAME (not at the zone apex)**, MX, NS, SOA, SRV, TXT, CAA, PTR.

Point an A, AAAA or CNAME record at an **Azure resource** (public IP, Traffic Manager, Front Door) so it **updates automatically** if the IP changes. Alias records **can be at the zone apex**, unlike CNAME.

Resolve names **only from VNets linked** to the zone. **Autoregistration** creates A records for **VMs** (primary NIC) in the linked VNet. A VNet can have **one registration zone**; a zone can have many registration VNets.

cards.front: Custom DNS server and private zones?
cards.back: If a VNet uses a **custom DNS server**, it **bypasses** Azure DNS and private zones. Forward to **168.63.129.16** (Azure-provided DNS) or use **Azure DNS Private Resolver**.

**Layer 4** (TCP/UDP). **Public** (internet-facing frontend) or **internal** (private frontend). Parts: **frontend IP**, **backend pool**, **health probe**, **load-balancing rule**, **inbound NAT rule**, **outbound rule**. Basic SKU **retired 30 Sept 2025**.

**Secure by default:** traffic needs an **NSG allow**. **Zone-redundant**, **99.99%** SLA, backend pool in **one VNet**, probes **TCP, HTTP, HTTPS**. Needs a **Standard public IP**. **HA ports** rule on internal LB balances all ports.
**None** (5-tuple hash, default), **Client IP** (2-tuple: source and destination IP), **Client IP and protocol** (3-tuple). Use Client IP when a user must keep hitting the same VM.

cards.front: Load Balancer vs Application Gateway vs Front Door?
cards.back: **Load Balancer:** regional Layer 4. **Application Gateway:** regional Layer 7 (URL path routing, TLS termination, **WAF**, cookie affinity, needs its own subnet). **Front Door:** **global** Layer 7 with CDN and WAF.

Check the **health probe** (backend must answer on the probe port/path; probes come from **168.63.129.16** and the **AzureLoadBalancer** tag must be allowed), the **NSG** allows client traffic (Standard), the backends are in the **pool**, and the app listens on the backend port. Use **Insights** metrics: Health Probe Status, Data Path Availability.

cards.front: Metrics vs logs in Azure Monitor?
cards.back: **Metrics:** numeric time series, near real time, lightweight, kept **93 days**; view in **Metrics explorer**. **Logs:** records of many types in a **Log Analytics workspace**, queried with **KQL**.

Subscription-level record of **control-plane** events (who created, changed or deleted what, service health). Kept **90 days**. Send it to a workspace with a diagnostic setting to keep longer or query with KQL.

Route a resource's **resource logs** and **platform metrics** to a **Log Analytics workspace**, a **storage account** (archive), **Event Hubs** (stream) or a partner. **Resource logs are not collected until you create one.**

Install the **Azure Monitor Agent (AMA)** and create a **data collection rule (DCR)** that says what to collect (performance counters, Windows events, Syslog) and where to send it. The old Log Analytics agent is **retired**. **VM insights** uses AMA.

`Heartbeat | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) | summarize count() by Computer`. Operators: **where** (filter), **summarize** (aggregate), **project** (choose columns), **take** (sample), **sort**, **render timechart**. Tables: Heartbeat, Perf, Event, Syslog, AzureActivity.

**Metric** (threshold on a metric), **Log search** (KQL query on a schedule), **Activity log** (an event such as VM deleted, plus **Service Health** and **Resource Health** alerts), Smart detection, Prometheus.

cards.front: Action group vs alert processing rule?
cards.back: **Action group:** *who and how* to notify or act (email, SMS, push, voice, webhook, Logic App, Function, Automation runbook, ITSM). **Alert processing rule:** changes **fired** alerts: **add action groups** or **suppress** notifications, at a scope, on a **schedule** (maintenance windows). Suppression wins over adding.

Curated views per service: **VM insights** (performance, map of dependencies), **Storage insights** (capacity, availability, latency), **Network insights** (topology, health). Built on metrics and logs.

**IP flow verify** (allowed or denied, and by which rule), **NSG diagnostics**, **Next hop**, **Effective security rules**, **Connection troubleshoot**, **Packet capture**, **VPN troubleshoot**. **Connection Monitor** tests connectivity **continuously** and alerts. **VNet flow logs** replace NSG flow logs (no new NSG flow logs since 30 June 2025).

cards.front: Recovery Services vault vs Backup vault?
cards.back: **Recovery Services vault:** **Azure VMs**, SQL and SAP HANA in VMs, **Azure Files**, MARS agent, MABS/DPM, and **Site Recovery**. **Backup vault:** **Azure Disks**, **Azure Blobs**, **Azure Database for PostgreSQL**, AKS.

Backup is **within a region**: the vault must be in the **same region** as the VMs it protects. You need a vault per region. Vaults can move between resource groups and subscriptions, **not regions**.

**Schedule** (Standard: once a day; **Enhanced**: multiple times a day, hourly) and **retention** (daily, weekly, monthly, yearly). **Instant restore** snapshots are kept locally for fast restores. One policy can protect many VMs.
**LRS, ZRS or GRS**. You can change it **only before** any items are backed up. **Cross Region Restore** (restore in the paired region any time) needs **GRS**.
**Create a new VM**, **restore disks** (then build a VM yourself), **replace existing** disks, or **file recovery** (a script mounts the recovery point so you copy files).

Deleted backup data is kept **14 days by default** (configurable **14-180**) at no cost for the first 14. **Enhanced soft delete** can be made **always-on**. You **cannot delete a vault** while it holds items, including soft-deleted ones.

cards.front: Azure Site Recovery for Azure VMs?
cards.back: **Replicates** VMs continuously to a **secondary region** (the Recovery Services vault is in the **target** region). Recovery points: **crash-consistent** (about every 5 minutes) and **app-consistent**. **Recovery plans** group VMs, set start order and add scripts.
**Test failover** into an isolated VNet (no impact; then **clean up**). **Failover** to a recovery point → **Commit** → **Re-protect** (replicate back to primary) → **Failback** → re-protect again.

**Backup reports** need **diagnostic settings** sending vault data to a **Log Analytics workspace**. **Built-in Azure Monitor alerts** fire for failures; route them with an **alert processing rule** and an **action group**. Metric alerts can alert on successful jobs.

questions.q: You need users from the Marketing department to be added to a group automatically when their department attribute is set. What should you create?
opts: A security group with assigned membership
A Microsoft 365 group with assigned membership
A security group with dynamic user membership
questions.why: Dynamic user membership evaluates a rule on user attributes. It needs Microsoft Entra ID P1.

questions.q: You try to assign a Microsoft 365 license to a new user and the option is unavailable. What should you set first?
questions.why: Usage location is required for license assignment because not every service is offered in every country.

questions.q: A partner company's staff need access to one of your apps. They must use their own company credentials. What should you do?
opts: Create a Microsoft 365 group for them
Sync their accounts with Microsoft Entra Connect
Invite them as B2B guest users
Create cloud-only member accounts for them
questions.why: B2B collaboration lets external users sign in with their own identity and appear as guests in your tenant.

questions.q: Which TWO can be members of a security group in Microsoft Entra ID?
questions.why: Security groups can contain users, devices, service principals and other groups. Azure resources are not members.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: You can manually add a user to a group that has dynamic user membership.
Group-based licensing removes the license when a user leaves the group.
A deleted user can be restored within 30 days.
questions.why: Dynamic groups are rule-only. Group licensing follows membership. Deleted users stay restorable for 30 days.

questions.q: You enable SSPR for a group named SSPR-Users. A Global Administrator who is not in the group forgets their password. What happens?
opts: Only another Global Administrator can reset it, by design
They cannot use SSPR until added to SSPR-Users
They can reset it with one method
They can reset it with two methods, because admins are always enabled for SSPR
questions.why: Administrator roles always have SSPR on with a two-gate policy, whatever the SSPR scope.

questions.q: Match each requirement to the group type or setting.
rows: Shared mailbox and Teams for a project
Grant an Azure role to a set of users
Members added by department attribute
All Windows devices added automatically
questions.why: Microsoft 365 groups are for collaboration. Security groups grant access. Dynamic rules can target users or devices, not both in one group.

questions.q: You need to create 500 user accounts from a spreadsheet with the least effort in the portal. What should you use?
opts: Bulk create with the CSV template
questions.why: Bulk create in the Entra admin center takes a CSV built from the template.

questions.q: Which license do you need to let cloud users reset forgotten passwords themselves?
opts: No license; it is included in every tenant
questions.why: SSPR reset needs P1 or higher. Changing a known password is free.

questions.q: A user must create and manage all resources in a resource group but must not grant access to others. Which role should you assign at the resource group?
questions.why: Contributor manages resources but cannot assign roles. Owner can assign roles.

questions.q: You assign Reader to User1 at the subscription and Contributor to User1 on RG1. What can User1 do on a VM in RG1?
questions.why: RBAC is additive. Contributor on RG1 is inherited by the VM.

questions.q: You must allow a help desk group to assign roles on RG1 without being able to change any resources. Which role is least privileged?
questions.why: RBAC Administrator can manage role assignments only. Owner can also change resources.

questions.q: Which TWO are valid scopes for an Azure role assignment?
questions.why: Azure RBAC scopes are management group, subscription, resource group and resource.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: A role assigned at a subscription is inherited by every resource group in it.
Contributor can assign roles to other users.
The Owner role always lets a user read blob data when using Microsoft Entra authorization.
questions.why: Inheritance flows down. Contributor cannot assign roles. Blob data access through Entra needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Reader.

questions.q: Match each need to the least-privileged built-in role.
rows: View everything, change nothing
Manage resources, no role assignments
Manage role assignments only
Read blobs with Entra ID
questions.why: Pick the smallest role that does the job.

questions.q: An app running on a VM must read secrets from Azure Key Vault without storing credentials. Which security principal should receive the role?
questions.why: A managed identity is a security principal Azure manages for the resource, so no secrets are stored.

questions.q: A user is Global Administrator in Microsoft Entra ID but cannot see any subscriptions. What can they do to manage access to all subscriptions?
opts: Add themselves to a Microsoft 365 group
Elevate access to become User Access Administrator at root scope
Assign themselves the Reader role in Entra ID
questions.why: Entra roles do not grant Azure resource access. Global Administrators can elevate access to the root scope.

questions.q: You must prevent anyone, including subscription Owners, from deleting a production resource group, while still allowing changes to its resources. What should you apply?
opts: A CanNotDelete lock on the resource group
A ReadOnly lock on the resource group
Remove the Owner role from all users
An Azure Policy with the Audit effect
questions.why: CanNotDelete blocks deletion but allows modification, and it applies to Owners too.

questions.q: You need to make sure resources can only be created in East US and West US. What should you use?
opts: Azure Policy with the Allowed locations definition
questions.why: Policy controls resource properties such as location, whatever role the creator has.

questions.q: A Department tag is set on RG1. A new storage account is created in RG1. What tags does the storage account have?
opts: None, unless a policy or the creator adds them
questions.why: Tags are not inherited. Use a Modify policy to inherit them.

questions.q: Which TWO policy effects can change or create resources through a remediation task?
questions.why: Modify and DeployIfNotExists use a managed identity and remediation tasks. Audit only reports, Deny only blocks.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: A ReadOnly lock on a resource group stops you from creating a new VM in it.
A budget automatically shuts down resources when the limit is reached.
Resources in a resource group can be in different regions from the group.
questions.why: ReadOnly blocks writes. Budgets alert and can trigger actions but do not stop resources by themselves. Resource group location only holds metadata.

questions.q: Match each requirement to the governance tool.
rows: Block VMs larger than a set size
Stop accidental deletion of a database
Alert when forecasted spend passes 80%
Recommend resizing underused VMs
questions.why: Policy shapes resources. Locks protect them. Budgets watch spend. Advisor recommends.

questions.q: You need to apply the same policies and role assignments to 30 subscriptions. What should you configure?
opts: A management group that contains the subscriptions
A resource group in each subscription
questions.why: Assignments at a management group are inherited by all subscriptions under it.

questions.q: A storage account has a ReadOnly lock. An admin with Owner tries to list the access keys in the portal and fails. Why?
opts: The lock is only on the resource group
Listing keys is a POST (write) operation that ReadOnly blocks
questions.why: List Keys is a POST action, so ReadOnly blocks it even for Owners.

questions.q: A contractor needs read access to one container for 48 hours. You must be able to revoke the access early without affecting other apps that use the account keys. What should you use?
opts: A service SAS that references a stored access policy
questions.why: Deleting or changing the stored access policy revokes the SAS without rotating keys.

questions.q: Which SAS type is signed with Microsoft Entra credentials and recommended by Microsoft?
questions.why: A user delegation SAS uses a key obtained with Entra credentials instead of the account key.

questions.q: VMs in Subnet1 must reach a storage account while all other networks are blocked. What should you configure on Subnet1 and the storage account?
opts: A Microsoft.Storage service endpoint and a virtual network rule
A NAT gateway and an IP rule for 10.0.1.0/24
A user-defined route to the internet
questions.why: Storage virtual network rules need the subnet's service endpoint. Private IP ranges cannot be used in IP rules.

questions.q: Which TWO identity sources can provide identity-based SMB access to Azure Files?
questions.why: Azure Files supports AD DS, Entra Domain Services and Entra Kerberos.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: A stored access policy can be used with a user delegation SAS.
A container can have up to five stored access policies.
Each storage account access key grants full access to the account.
questions.why: Stored access policies work with service SAS only. Five per container. Account keys are all-powerful.

questions.q: Match each requirement to the access method.
rows: Revoke many SAS tokens without changing keys
SAS signed with Entra credentials
One SAS for blobs and queues together
Grant an SMB share to an AD group
choices: Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor
questions.why: Pick by what signs the token and what it covers.

questions.q: Users mount an Azure file share with AD credentials. They can connect but get Access denied on one folder. Share-level roles are correct. What should you check?
opts: The NTFS permissions on the folder
questions.why: After the share-level check, Windows ACLs decide directory and file access.

questions.q: An ad hoc service SAS signed with key1 has leaked. There is no stored access policy. What revokes it immediately?
questions.why: Without a policy, the only way to invalidate the signature is to rotate the key that signed it.

questions.q: Data must survive the loss of an entire Azure region and be readable from the secondary region at any time. Which redundancy should you choose?
questions.why: RA-GRS replicates to the paired region and allows reads from the secondary without failover. GRS needs failover first.

questions.q: You need the lowest-cost redundancy that survives the failure of one datacenter (zone) in the region. What should you choose?
questions.why: ZRS copies across zones. LRS stays in one datacenter. Geo options cost more.

questions.q: You plan object replication from storage1 to storage2. Which TWO settings are required on storage1?
questions.why: The source needs versioning and change feed. The destination needs versioning.

questions.q: You must use your own keys to encrypt a storage account. Where must the key be stored?
opts: In the storage account's access keys
Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM
questions.why: Customer-managed keys live in Key Vault or Managed HSM, with soft delete and purge protection on.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: You can turn off encryption at rest for a standard storage account.
Infrastructure (double) encryption can be enabled after the account is created.
Premium file shares support zone-redundant storage.
questions.why: Encryption is always on. Infrastructure encryption is set at creation. Premium supports LRS and ZRS.

questions.q: Match each copy of data to the redundancy option.
rows: 3 copies in one datacenter
3 copies across availability zones
Copies in the paired region, readable any time
Zone copies plus a paired region copy
questions.why: Count where the copies live.

questions.q: You need to copy 2 TB from an on-premises file server to a blob container from a script, and re-run it later copying only changes. What should you use?
questions.why: AzCopy is scriptable and azcopy sync copies only differences.

questions.q: Which storage account type should you choose for Azure file shares that need consistent low latency on SSDs?
questions.why: Premium file shares are the SSD account kind for Azure Files.

questions.q: Blobs are rarely read after 30 days and never after 180 days, but must be kept for 7 years. You need to minimize cost automatically. What should you configure?
opts: A lifecycle management rule that moves blobs to Cool, then Archive
questions.why: Lifecycle rules tier and delete blobs by age automatically.

questions.q: A user needs to read an archived blob within one hour. What should you do?
opts: Create a snapshot of the blob
Change the blob tier to Hot with high rehydration priority
Read the blob directly from the Archive tier
questions.why: Archive is offline. High priority rehydration usually completes in under an hour.

questions.q: Users accidentally overwrite important blobs. You need to restore the previous content automatically kept on each write. What should you enable?
questions.why: Versioning keeps the previous version on every write. Soft delete protects against deletes.

questions.q: Which TWO features let you recover a deleted Azure file share or a file in it?
questions.why: Share soft delete restores the share. Snapshots restore earlier versions of files.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Archive tier can be set as the default access tier of a storage account.
Moving a blob out of Cool after 10 days can incur an early deletion charge.
Point-in-time restore for block blobs requires versioning, change feed and soft delete.
questions.why: Archive is per blob only. Cool has a 30-day minimum. PITR needs all three.

questions.q: Match each requirement to the feature.
rows: Keep files local on a branch office server
Restore a folder from yesterday's share copy
Lock records so no one can delete them for 7 years
Delete logs older than 90 days
questions.why: Each feature has one job.

questions.q: You set a container's access level to Blob, but anonymous users still get an error. What is the likely cause?
opts: The blobs are in the Hot tier
Anonymous access is disallowed on the storage account
The container has a stored access policy
questions.why: Allow Blob anonymous access must be enabled on the account before container-level public access works.

questions.q: Which access tier has a 180-day minimum and is offline?
questions.why: Archive is the cheapest storage, 180-day minimum, and must be rehydrated before reading.

questions.q: You have an ARM template in JSON and want to maintain it in Bicep. Which command should you run?
questions.why: Decompile converts JSON to Bicep. Build does the reverse.

questions.q: You deploy a template to RG1 in Complete mode. RG1 contains a VM that is not in the template. What happens to the VM?
questions.why: Complete mode removes resources in the group that the template does not define.

questions.q: Which section of an ARM template is required in every template?
questions.why: Only $schema, contentVersion and resources are required.

questions.q: You need to preview which resources a deployment will create, change or delete without deploying. What should you run?
questions.why: What-if shows the predicted changes before you deploy.

questions.q: Which TWO ways give you a template for resources that already exist in a resource group?
opts: Open the template from the resource group's deployment history
Export template from the resource group
questions.why: Export captures current state. Deployment history shows what was deployed.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: Incremental is the default deployment mode.
Bicep needs a state file to track deployed resources, like Terraform.
A parameter marked @secure() is not written to the deployment history.
questions.why: Incremental is default. Bicep has no state file. Secure parameter values are not logged.

questions.q: Match each template part to its job.
rows: Values supplied at deployment time
Values computed inside the template
The things to create
Values returned after deployment
questions.why: Inputs, internals, resources, results.

questions.q: A template creates a storage account and needs a globally unique name that stays the same on every redeploy to the same resource group. Which function should you use?
questions.why: uniqueString is deterministic for the same input. newGuid changes every time.

questions.q: A Bicep file deploys a VM that references a NIC by its symbolic name. Do you need to add dependsOn?
opts: No, because NICs are deployed last
Yes, but only in Complete mode
No, Bicep adds the dependency from the reference
questions.why: Referencing another resource's symbolic name creates an implicit dependency.

questions.q: You try to resize VM1 but the size you need does not appear in the list. What should you do first?
opts: Move VM1 to another resource group
questions.why: Sizes not available on the current cluster appear after the VM is deallocated.

questions.q: An app stores data on the D: drive of a Windows VM. After maintenance the data is gone. Why?
opts: The VM was in an availability set
D: is the temporary disk, which is not persistent
The data disk was Standard HDD
questions.why: Temporary disks are lost on deallocation, redeploy or host move.

questions.q: You need the highest SLA for two VMs running the same app in one region. How should you deploy them?
questions.why: Zones give 99.99%. Availability sets give 99.95%.

questions.q: You are deploying new VMs that must have encrypted temp disks and caches. Azure Disk Encryption is retiring. What should you enable?
opts: Infrastructure encryption on a storage account
questions.why: Encryption at host covers temp disks and caches and replaces ADE.

questions.q: You need to move a VM from West Europe to North Europe. Which service should you use?
questions.why: Moving between resource groups or subscriptions keeps the region. Resource Mover moves across regions.

questions.q: Which TWO statements about availability sets are true?
opts: They protect against a full datacenter failure
A VM must be added to the set when it is created
They spread VMs across up to 3 fault domains
questions.why: Availability sets protect within a datacenter (99.95%). Zones protect against datacenter loss (99.99%).

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if it is true. Otherwise, select No.
stmts: You can reduce the size of a managed disk from 256 GiB to 128 GiB.
Ultra Disks can be used as OS disks.
Moving a VM to another resource group changes its resource ID.
questions.why: Disks can only grow. Ultra Disks are data disks only. The resource ID includes the resource group.

questions.q: Match each workload to the VM family.
rows: Web server that idles most of the day
In-memory database cache
Batch math with high CPU
Machine learning training on GPUs
questions.why: B burst, E memory, F compute, N GPU.

questions.q: A scale set must add VMs when average CPU is above 75% and remove them below 25%, never going under 2 VMs. What should you configure?
opts: Autoscale with scale-out and scale-in rules and a minimum of 2
An availability set with 2 fault domains
questions.why: Metric rules with min/max counts automate scaling.

questions.q: You need an Azure Container Registry with replicas in three regions and access only over private endpoints. Which SKU is required?
opts: Any SKU with the admin user enabled
questions.why: Geo-replication and private endpoints are Premium features.

questions.q: A containerized API must scale to zero when idle and scale out based on HTTP traffic. What should you use?
questions.why: Container Apps uses KEDA to scale on HTTP requests and supports scale to zero.

questions.q: A container in ACI needs more memory. What must you do?

**Initiative** = group of definitions. Assign at a scope with **exclusions**.

**Tags are not inherited.** Use a Modify policy to inherit them.
**Management groups** up to six levels deep. **Budgets** alert but do not stop resources. **Advisor** recommends savings.

Deleting a resource group deletes everything in it.
